title: When the Drop Wakes
premise: Sebastian Voss, a gifted interpreter embedded in a doomed peace delegation, has spent a decade erasing her past as a signals analyst for an intelligence service that disavowed her. When a voiceprint she recorded years ago unlocks a server in Singapore containing proof that the peace talks were engineered to collapse for market gain, she becomes the only living key to the truth. Hunted by an assassin contracted by the consortium behind the scheme and obstructed by three governments who each want the evidence buried or weaponized, Voss must decide whether loyalty to her old handler outweighs the truth. She smuggles the decryption to Frankfurt and releases it minutes before markets open, toppling the consortium at the cost of her anonymity—and finally reclaiming her real name.
about_author: Wendell Ishikawa is a former conference interpreter turned novelist who has worked behind the glass at summits on four continents. He writes thrillers about people whose professions demand perfect silence.

chapters.title: The Go-Bag
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. In Geneva, she interprets the opening session of peace talks she privately believes are theater, cataloguing exits and keeping her packed bag under the hotel bed. The beat is controlled dread: competence as camouflage, and the first hint that someone in the delegation recognizes her voice.

chapters.title: A Voice Like a Key
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. A technician asks her to record calibration audio for the summit's secure comms; the phrase he chooses is one she last spoke years ago in another life. That night her room is searched with surgical precision. Emotional beat: the past knocking on a door she thought she'd bricked over.

chapters.title: Singapore Answers
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Her old calibration phrase triggers an automated dead-drop server in Singapore, forwarding her a fragment: transaction records tying the talks' collapse to a Frankfurt trading desk. She realizes her voice was harvested as a failsafe key. Beat: vertigo—she was never invisible, just dormant.

chapters.title: The Handler's Warning
chapters.summary: Marcus Hale's POV. Voss's former intelligence handler, now a consultant, receives an alert that 'the asset' has resurfaced and is ordered to contain her—or deliver her. He warns her obliquely through a coded classified ad. Beat: divided loyalties; Hale loves her like family and is paid to betray her.

chapters.title: Assassin's Ledger
chapters.summary: The assassin Ilse Brandt's POV. Brandt reviews the contract on 'the Interpreter,' noting the client wants it quiet, before markets open Friday. She studies Voss's file and finds gaps even she wasn't given. Beat: professional curiosity curdling into suspicion about who the real target is.

chapters.title: Dead Language
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. She decodes the server fragment using an obscure dialect only she and one dead colleague spoke, uncovering a second layer: names of officials in all three governments on the consortium's payroll. Beat: the truth is bigger and more radioactive than survival allows.

chapters.title: Geneva Lockdown
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. A delegate dies of an apparent heart attack after asking too many questions; security locks down the summit and Voss realizes the talks aren't failing—they're being executed. She copies the server data to a microdot inside her interpreting headset. Beat: grief hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Three Flags
chapters.summary: Alternating POV vignettes: a minister in Berlin, a colonel in Washington, a director in Beijing each learn the server exists and quietly move to seize it. Beat: cold institutional menace—the truth has three owners and none of them is justice.

chapters.title: Train to Basel
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. She slips the lockdown during a plenary break, riding a train toward Basel while Brandt boards two cars back. A tense cat-and-mouse through the dining car ends with Voss swapping coats with a stranger. Beat: adrenaline and the loneliness of running.

chapters.title: What Marcus Owes
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Flashback to the operation years ago when Voss's unit was burned and disavowed—Hale signed the order that erased her name. Present-day: he stalls his own agency to buy her forty-eight hours. Beat: guilt as debt, love as liability.

chapters.title: Safehouse Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. In a Basel safehouse she calculates odds: three governments want silence, one assassin wants closure, and the market opens in fifty-one hours. She drafts the release but hesitates—the file also exposes the dead colleague's role. Beat: truth versus the memory of someone she loved.

chapters.title: Brandt's Doubt
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. She corners Voss in a cathedral, blade to ribs, but Voss shows her proof that the consortium plans to erase Brandt as loose end number two. Brandt lets her walk—an unforgivable professional sin. Beat: the assassin's identity crisis begins.

chapters.title: The Frankfurt Desk
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Following the money, she infiltrates a data center outside Frankfurt where the consortium's trades were staged, photographing hardware manifests. An alarm trips; she escapes through cooling tunnels. Beat: from fugitive to hunter—the story turns offensive.

chapters.title: Governments Negotiate
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. The three governments meet secretly and agree to jointly suppress the server rather than let any rival control it. Hale votes yes and immediately leaks the meeting time to Voss. Beat: betrayal of institutions in service of a person—the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Interrogation of One
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Captured briefly by Berlin's counterintelligence, she talks her way out by interpreting their own intercepted chatter back at them, revealing a mole among the interrogators. Released as a liability, not an ally. Beat: her skill—language—as literal weapon.

chapters.title: Loose Ends
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Ordered to finish the job and then disappear, Brandt instead feeds Voss the client's dead-drop schedule. Her handler notices the anomaly. Beat: defection in motion, priced in blood.

chapters.title: Night Before Markets
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Thursday night: she and Brandt stage the release infrastructure while Hale distracts surveillance with a decoy handoff. Voss records the final authentication phrase—her own voice, chosen this time. Beat: quiet before detonation; agency reclaimed.

chapters.title: The Decoy Handoff
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. The decoy goes wrong; Hale is taken by the consortium's fixers and interrogated for Voss's location. He gives them a true statement that is nonetheless useless—a lifetime of tradecraft spent in one sentence. Beat: sacrifice without heroics.

chapters.title: Open Outcry
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. 8:55 a.m., Frankfurt. From a rented office above the exchange she executes the release: files cascade to regulators, exchanges, and newsrooms as the opening bell rings. Consortium stocks crater in ninety seconds. Beat: catharsis—the truth hits the tape.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Brandt confronts her handler in a parking structure and walks away alive but exiled, choosing to vanish rather than be cleaned up. Beat: the assassin refuses to be anyone's instrument again—identity as choice.

chapters.title: Hale's Silence
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. She extracts Hale from custody using leverage gleaned from the released files, but he declines to run with her, staying to face inquiry on his own terms. Their farewell is in a language no one else in the café speaks. Beat: loyalty honored, not requited; grief with dignity.

chapters.title: Her Own Name
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Weeks later, in Lisbon, Sebastian Voss unpacks the go-bag for the first time in a decade and mails its contents—old identities—to a journalist. Under her birth name, she takes work interpreting for a refugee tribunal. Beat: resolution—invisibility traded for authorship of her own life; the drop has woken.
